h1: AC Repair in Clear Lake, Houston
title: AC Repair Clear Lake, Houston | AC Repair Houston
description: Tract houses and newer subdivisions on low bay land, where a flooded back yard puts the air handler and the condensate line in wet ground level space.
intro: Clear Lake is low ground, and low ground changes air conditioning. Much of this area sits a few feet above the bay with a water table close under the surface, so a heavy storm puts water in back yards and along the low side of the house, right where the equipment has to stay dry. The cooling problems here are less about how old the system is and more about where the system is sitting.
localAngle: The housing runs from 1960s and 70s ranch tracts through 80s and 90s subdivisions and into newer builds on the bay side. Roofs are asphalt shingle at a low pitch, so there is little attic space, and on the older ranches the air handler lives in a garage or a low closet off the utility room. The ground is the problem: sandy, close to the water table and slow to drain. After a storm the yard ponds, the pad under the outdoor unit sits in water, and the condensate line has nowhere to go but back into the pan.
commonCalls: Outdoor units standing in ponded back yard water after a storm, with corrosion starting at the base
Condensate lines that back up because the drain outlet is below the flood line in the yard
Air handlers in garage and utility closets where the base of the cabinet is damp or wet
Systems that run but will not cool after the ground around the unit stays wet for days
Newer homes where the outdoor unit was set on a slab that now drains toward the house

faqs.q: My back yard floods every storm. Is my outdoor unit in danger?
faqs.a: It depends on how long the water sits and whether the unit is submerged. A few hours of standing water with the base of the cabinet in it will start eating the metal and get into the electrical connections. A unit that sits in water for a day is a different situation entirely. The fix is usually to raise the equipment onto a pedestal or a curb so the base clears the high water line, and that is worth doing before the next storm rather than after one.

faqs.q: Why does my unit stop cooling after it rains?
faqs.a: Two common causes. If the unit is standing in water, the coil is running at a lower temperature because the wet ground is pulling heat out of it, and the controls can shut the system down or limit the compressor. If the indoor coil is the problem, a humid house after a wet spell loads the coil with much more moisture than usual, and a marginal system that was coping in dry August now freezes or barely dehumidifies. Which one you have comes down to whether the air leaving the vents is cold and wet or merely cold.

faqs.q: Should the condensate drain exit somewhere else?
faqs.a: On a lot where the yard floods, the standard exit near the foundation is a poor choice. Moving the outlet to a line that runs to a street drain or to a sump gets the water off the property before the yard ponds. It has to fall the whole way, so the pipe route matters, and it may mean reworking the line rather than just extending it. The company that covers this area can look at the existing run and tell you how it was sloped.

faqs.q: I live in one of the newer subdivisions. Do I have the same problems?
faqs.a: Not the same ones. Newer construction in this area means better duct sealing, a properly sized unit and equipment set above grade on a raised pad, so the common calls here are narrower. The persistent issue on new lots is fill dirt. Builders bring in soil that drains badly for the first few wet seasons, and that shows up as a yard that ponds or a slab edge that lets water sit against the foundation. If your system is new and performing, the odds are the problem is drainage rather than the machine.
